kind.speaker: Speaker
band.good.title: Good
band.good.summary: Nothing on your network stands out as an easy way in.
band.fair.title: Fair
band.fair.summary: A few things are worth tightening up.
band.poor.title: Needs work
band.poor.summary: Some devices are easier to get into than they should be, so work through the risks listed below.
band.bad.title: At risk
band.bad.summary: Some devices are open to anyone on your network, so start with the first risks listed below.
rule.telnet-open.title: Telnet is switched on
rule.telnet-open.why: Telnet is an old way to control a device by typing commands over the network. Everything it sends, passwords included, travels as plain text, and devices that offer it often have a default password that is easy to guess.
rule.telnet-open.fix: Open the device's admin page or app and switch off Telnet (port {port}). It is usually under Administration, Security or Remote Access. If you need remote control, use SSH instead. If there is no such setting, install the latest firmware update, and if the modem came from your internet provider, ask them to turn Telnet off.
rule.ftp-open.title: FTP file sharing is switched on
rule.ftp-open.why: FTP is an old way to share files over the network. It sends passwords and files as plain text, and some devices let anyone in without a password at all.
rule.ftp-open.fix: If you do not use it, switch off the FTP server (port {port}) in the device's settings, often under file sharing or services. If you need it, use SFTP instead and set a strong password.
rule.vnc-no-auth.title: Screen sharing without a password
rule.vnc-no-auth.why: VNC lets someone see and control this device's screen over the network. It asks for no password, so anyone on your network can take over the screen, keyboard and mouse.
rule.vnc-no-auth.fix: Open the screen sharing or VNC settings on the device and set a strong password, or switch the feature off (port {port}) if you do not use it. On a Mac it is in System Settings, General, Sharing, Screen Sharing.
rule.vnc-open.title: Screen sharing is switched on
rule.vnc-open.why: VNC lets someone see and control this device's screen over the network. Even with a password, older VNC logins only check the first eight characters of it, and the connection is often not encrypted.
rule.vnc-open.fix: If you do not use it, switch screen sharing off (port {port}). If you do, choose a long password and turn the feature on only when you need it. To reach it from outside your home, use a VPN instead of opening a port on the router.
rule.rdp-open.title: Remote Desktop is switched on
rule.rdp-open.why: Remote Desktop lets someone sign in to this Windows computer from another device. With strong passwords it is fine at home, but it is a common target for password guessing, especially once it can be reached from the internet.
rule.rdp-open.fix: If you do not use it, switch it off in Settings, System, Remote Desktop (port {port}). If you do, give every account a strong password and make sure the router does not forward this port to the internet.
rule.adb-open.title: Android debugging is open to anyone
rule.adb-open.why: ADB is a developer tool for Android phones, TVs and TV boxes. It is switched on here and accepts commands without any approval, so anyone on your network could install apps, read files or take full control of the device.
rule.adb-open.fix: Open the device's settings, go to Developer options and switch off USB debugging and wireless debugging (port {port}). If a TV box has no such option, or the setting comes back after a restart, its software cannot be trusted and replacing the box is the safest choice.
rule.adb-exposed.title: Android debugging is switched on
rule.adb-exposed.why: ADB is a developer tool for Android phones, TVs and TV boxes, and it is switched on here. Even when the device asks for approval before it accepts commands, anyone on your network can make the approval prompt appear, and one accidental tap on Allow gives them full control.
rule.adb-exposed.fix: Unless you develop apps, open Developer options in the device's settings and switch off USB debugging and wireless debugging (port {port}). Never approve a debugging request you did not start yourself.
rule.redis-no-auth.title: Redis database without a password
rule.redis-no-auth.why: Redis is a database that programs use to store data. This one lets anyone on your network read and change everything in it, and an open Redis can often be used to take over the computer it runs on.
rule.redis-no-auth.fix: Set a password with the requirepass setting in redis.conf, or make Redis listen only on the computer itself (bind 127.0.0.1), then restart it (port {port}). If it came with an app or a Docker container, change the setting there.
rule.docker-api-open.title: Docker remote control is open to anyone
rule.docker-api-open.why: The Docker API lets programs start and manage containers on this computer. It answers without a password, which gives anyone on your network full control of the machine.
rule.docker-api-open.fix: Remove the tcp:// listener (port {port}) from the Docker daemon settings, either daemon.json or the -H option of the service, and restart Docker. If you need remote access, use SSH or TLS with client certificates instead.
rule.memcached-open.title: Memcached is open to the network
rule.memcached-open.why: Memcached is a cache that programs use to keep data in memory. It has no passwords by default, so anyone on your network can read what is stored in it, and if it can be reached from the internet it can be abused to attack other sites.
rule.memcached-open.fix: Make memcached listen only on the computer itself: start it with -l 127.0.0.1 or put that in its configuration file, then restart it (port {port}). If an app or container brought it along, change the setting there.
rule.elasticsearch-no-auth.title: Elasticsearch without a password
rule.elasticsearch-no-auth.why: Elasticsearch is a search database. This one answers anyone on your network without a password, so everything stored in it can be read, changed or deleted.
rule.elasticsearch-no-auth.fix: Turn on the built-in security in elasticsearch.yml (xpack.security.enabled: true) and set passwords, or make it listen only on the computer itself (network.host: 127.0.0.1), then restart it (port {port}).
rule.database-open.title: Database reachable from the network
rule.database-open.why: This device runs a database server ({service}) that accepts connections from every device on your network. If its password is weak or still the default, the data in it can be read or changed.
rule.database-open.fix: If only programs on this computer use it, make the database listen on 127.0.0.1 only (port {port}). Otherwise give every account a strong password and make sure the router does not forward this port to the internet.
rule.mqtt-anonymous.title: Smart home messages open to anyone
rule.mqtt-anonymous.why: MQTT is a messaging system that smart home devices use to send readings and receive commands. This one lets anyone on your network connect without a password, so they could read sensor data or switch devices on and off.
rule.mqtt-anonymous.fix: In the MQTT broker settings, for example Mosquitto or the Home Assistant add-on, turn off anonymous access (allow_anonymous false in Mosquitto) and give each device its own user name and password (port {port}).
rule.rtsp-no-auth.title: Camera video plays without a password
rule.rtsp-no-auth.why: RTSP is how cameras and video recorders send live video. This stream opens without a password, so anyone on your network can watch it.
rule.rtsp-no-auth.fix: In the camera's app or admin page, turn on authentication for RTSP or video streaming and change the default password (port {port}). Then check for a firmware update.
rule.smb1-enabled.title: Old SMB1 file sharing is switched on
rule.smb1-enabled.why: SMB1 is the original, decades-old version of Windows file sharing. It has well-known security holes, and the WannaCry ransomware used it in 2017 to spread from computer to computer.
rule.smb1-enabled.fix: Switch SMB1 off on this device (port {port}). On a NAS or router it is usually a minimum SMB version in the file sharing settings: choose SMB2 or later. On Windows, open Turn Windows features on or off and untick SMB 1.0/CIFS File Sharing Support. If an old printer or TV still needs SMB1, it is time to update or replace it.
rule.socks-no-auth.title: Open proxy without a password
rule.socks-no-auth.why: A SOCKS proxy passes internet traffic along for other devices. This one does it for anyone, without a password. If it can be reached from the internet, strangers can send their traffic through your connection and it will look as if it came from you.
rule.socks-no-auth.fix: Find the program or device that runs the proxy (port {port}) and turn on a password, or switch it off. Make sure the router does not forward this port to the internet. If nobody at home set up a proxy, treat it as a warning sign: update the device, reset it to factory settings if needed, and change its password.
rule.dvr-port-open.title: Video recorder service is reachable
rule.dvr-port-open.why: Many low-cost cameras and video recorders talk to their phone apps over port {port}. The software behind it has a long record of security holes and hidden default passwords.
rule.dvr-port-open.fix: Install the latest firmware from the maker's website, change the default password, and make sure the router does not forward this port to the internet. If the maker no longer releases updates, move the recorder to a separate guest network or replace it.
rule.winbox-open.title: MikroTik Winbox management is reachable
rule.winbox-open.why: Winbox is the management tool for MikroTik routers. Anyone who can reach it can try to log in, and old RouterOS versions had a hole that let attackers read the admin password without logging in.
rule.winbox-open.fix: Update RouterOS to the latest version and use a strong admin password. Under IP, Services, limit Winbox (port {port}) to the computers you manage the router from, or switch it off, and make sure it can never be reached from the internet.
rule.pptp-open.title: Old PPTP VPN is switched on
rule.pptp-open.why: PPTP is an old type of VPN for reaching your home network from outside. Its encryption was broken years ago, so someone who captures the traffic can recover the password and what was sent.
rule.pptp-open.fix: Switch off the PPTP VPN server on the router's admin page (port {port}). If the router offers a modern VPN such as WireGuard or OpenVPN, use that instead.
rule.webmin-open.title: Webmin admin panel is reachable
rule.webmin-open.why: Webmin is a web page for managing a whole server: users, files and services. Anyone on your network can reach its login page, and older Webmin versions had serious security holes.
rule.webmin-open.fix: Update Webmin to the latest version and use a strong password with two-step login. In Webmin's IP Access Control, allow only the computers you manage it from (port {port}), and never forward it to the internet.
rule.nfs-open.title: NFS file sharing is reachable
rule.nfs-open.why: NFS is a way to share folders, common on NAS boxes and Linux. It usually trusts any device that connects instead of asking for a password, so a share that is not limited to certain devices can be read by anyone on your network.
rule.nfs-open.fix: In the NAS or server settings, limit each NFS share to the addresses of the devices that need it and make shares read-only where you can. If you only use Windows or Mac file sharing, switch NFS off (port {port}).
rule.rsync-open.title: rsync file sharing is reachable
rule.rsync-open.why: rsync is a tool for copying and backing up files, often found on NAS boxes. It shares folders over the network, sometimes without a password.
rule.rsync-open.fix: If you do not use it for backups, switch off the rsync service in the NAS or server settings (port {port}). If you do, give every shared folder a user name and password and allow only the devices that run your backups.
rule.login-over-http.title: Login page without encryption
rule.login-over-http.why: This device asks for a password on a web page that does not use HTTPS. The login and everything on the page travel unencrypted, so another device on your network or someone on your Wi-Fi could capture the password, or enough to work it out.
rule.login-over-http.fix: If the device offers HTTPS, use it and switch off plain HTTP access (port {port}). If it does not, choose a password you use nowhere else and log in only over a connection you trust. A firmware update sometimes adds HTTPS.
rule.old-tls.title: Outdated encryption
rule.old-tls.why: This device still uses {version}, a version of the encryption that was retired in 2021 because of known weaknesses. Modern browsers and apps may refuse to connect, and the connection is less private than it should be.
rule.old-tls.fix: Check for a firmware update from the maker, which often adds TLS 1.2 or newer (port {port}). If the settings let you pick a minimum TLS version, choose 1.2. This is not urgent on a home network.
rule.upnp-igd.title: Devices can open ports on the router
rule.upnp-igd.why: UPnP lets any device at home ask the router to open a port, a way in from the internet, without asking you. Games and video calls use it, but so can malware on an infected device, and many cameras open themselves to the internet this way.
rule.upnp-igd.fix: On the router's admin page, look for UPnP, often under Advanced, NAT or Network, and switch it off. If a game console or app stops working afterwards, add a port forward just for it, or turn UPnP back on and check its list of open ports from time to time.
rule.tr069-open.title: Provider remote management is reachable
rule.tr069-open.why: TR-069 is how internet providers manage their modems remotely: updates, settings and fault checks. Here it also answers on your home network, which is usually harmless but is one more service that could have bugs.
rule.tr069-open.fix: This is usually controlled by your internet provider, so you often cannot switch it off yourself (port {port}). Keep the modem's firmware up to date, and ask your provider whether remote management can be limited.
rule.jetdirect-open.title: Printer accepts jobs from any device
rule.jetdirect-open.why: This printer accepts print jobs on port {port} from any device on your network, without a password. That is normal for home printers; the main risk is someone printing junk or, on some models, changing settings.
rule.jetdirect-open.fix: Usually nothing to do. If you like, update the printer's firmware and set an admin password on its web page or in its app. If all your devices print through AirPrint or IPP, you can switch off raw printing, often called RAW or JetDirect.
rule.smb-open.title: File sharing (SMB) is switched on
rule.smb-open.why: SMB is the standard way computers and NAS boxes share files and printers. It is normal at home; it is listed so you know which devices share files.
rule.smb-open.fix: Nothing to do if you share files on purpose. Make sure every share needs a password and that the router does not forward port {port} to the internet. If you never share files from this device, you can switch file sharing off.
rule.ssh-open.title: SSH remote login is switched on
rule.ssh-open.why: SSH lets someone log in to this device and run commands over an encrypted connection. It is safe with strong passwords or keys, and common on NAS boxes, small computers like the Raspberry Pi, and routers.
rule.ssh-open.fix: Nothing to do if you use it. Use a strong password or SSH keys, keep the device updated, and do not forward port {port} to the internet unless you have to. If you do not use it, switch it off in the device's settings.
rule.unknown-device.title: Device we could not identify
rule.unknown-device.why: We could not tell what this device is. That is common for smart plugs, bulbs and other small gadgets, and for phones that hide their identity, but it is good to know every device on your network.
rule.unknown-device.fix: Check the list of connected devices on the router's admin page or app, which often shows device names. If you do not recognize it, change your Wi-Fi password and reconnect your own devices one by one.
rule.port-forward-risky.title: Risky port open to the internet
rule.port-forward-risky.why: The router forwards port {external_port} from the internet straight to port {internal_port} on this device, so anyone on the internet can reach it directly. This port is used by the kind of service that attackers search the whole internet for, like remote desktop, file sharing, cameras or databases. Devices can set up forwards like this on their own through UPnP, without asking you.
rule.port-forward-risky.fix: Remove this forward. On the router's admin page, find the UPnP or Port Forwarding section, often under Advanced or NAT, and delete the entry for port {external_port}. On most routers, switching UPnP off removes forwards like this automatically. Do not keep this one even if a game or app asked for it: to reach the device from outside your home, use a VPN instead.
rule.port-forward.title: Port open to the internet
rule.port-forward.why: The router forwards port {external_port} from the internet straight to port {internal_port} on this device, so anyone on the internet can reach it directly. Devices can set up forwards like this on their own through UPnP, without asking you. Game consoles, video calls and some apps do this all the time and it is usually fine, but it is good to know which devices can be reached from outside.
rule.port-forward.fix: If you know what set it up, for example a game console, you can leave it. If not, open the router's admin page, find the UPnP or Port Forwarding section, often under Advanced or NAT, and delete the entry for port {external_port}. On most routers, switching UPnP off removes forwards like this automatically.
rule.double-nat.title: Router behind another router
rule.double-nat.why: Your router's internet address, {external_ip}, is a private one. That means it is not connected to the internet directly but through another router, often the modem from your internet provider. This is usually fine for safety, but connections from outside stop at the first router, so port forwards and some online games, voice chats or remote access apps may not work.
rule.double-nat.fix: If everything works, there is nothing to do. If games or port forwards give you trouble, put the provider's modem in bridge mode so that only your own router handles the connection. If you cannot find that setting, ask your provider to do it.
rule.cgnat.title: Internet address shared with other customers
rule.cgnat.why: Your router's internet address, {external_ip}, comes from a range that providers use to share one public address between many customers (CGNAT). Nothing on the internet can reach your home network directly, which is good for safety, but it also means port forwarding cannot work, and some games or remote access apps may have trouble connecting.
rule.cgnat.fix: Usually nothing to do. If you need port forwarding, for example to reach a camera from outside or to run a game server, ask your provider for a public IP address. Some providers give one on request, sometimes for a fee.
ui.no_network: No local network found. Are you connected to Wi-Fi or a cable?
ui.sandbox.wsl: This looks like WSL. In its default mode WSL sits on a virtual network, not your home network. Run Hearthscan on Windows itself, or switch WSL to mirrored networking.
ui.sandbox.container: Hearthscan is running in a container, so this is probably the container's network, not your home network.
ui.network.narrowed: {network} (the network is large, so only your part of it)
ui.router.title: Your router
ui.router.none: No ports are opened to the internet through UPnP.
ui.router.no_upnp: The router does not answer UPnP questions, so there is nothing more to read from it. That is fine: it also means devices cannot open ports on it by themselves.
ui.router.incomplete: The router did not list all of its forwards, so there may be more than shown here.

gui.window_missing: The window needs pywebview (pip install hearthscan[window]); opening your browser instead.
gui.window_failed: The window could not be opened ({reason}); opening your browser instead.
gui.start.title: What is on your network?
gui.start.body: Hearthscan finds the devices on your network, checks each one for common risks and tells you in plain words what to do about them.
gui.start.safe: It only looks: nothing on your devices is changed, and only private networks such as your home network are checked.
gui.start.ports_only_hint: Quicker, but the services behind the ports are not checked, so some risks may be missed.
gui.scan.title: Checking your network
gui.scan.hint: This can take a few minutes. Nothing on your devices is changed.
gui.error.token: This page only works through the link Hearthscan opens for you. Start Hearthscan again to get a new one.
gui.connection.lost: Lost the connection to Hearthscan. Trying again.
gui.result.unprobed: Services were not checked, so the score may look better than it is.
gui.result.privacy: A saved report lists the addresses and device names on your network. Share it only with people you trust.
gui.save.started: Saving {name}. If it does not show up in your downloads, copy it instead.
gui.save.copied: Copied. Paste it into a text editor and save it as {name}.
gui.save.copy_failed: Copying did not work either. Select all of the text below, copy it and save it as {name}.
